extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners (and patent applicants/agents prosecuting applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and communicating lack of unity of invention in patent applications, including when and how to identify the defect, how to group claims, responses and elections, referrals, and special considerations (Markush groups, intermediates, multi-step methods, provisos, divisional applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explaining a lack of unity defect
rubrics_metrics.description: A report identifying a lack of unity of invention should explain the basis for the conclusion so the applicant can decide whether and how to limit or divide their claims for further examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanation should identify what the examiner considers the distinct inventions to be and provide sufficient detail for the applicant to understand why the different inventions do not share a single general inventive concept. Where the defect is identified a posteriori, cite the prior art supporting this conclusion and explain the significance of each document. Wherever possible, relate the individual inventions to the claims in which they are defined so the applicant can group claims into sets viewed as sharing a single general inventive concept. Generally set out groups of claims considered to be directed to one invention only and indicate to which group each independent claim belongs. Unless explicitly indicated otherwise, dependent claims are presumed to belong to the group in which the claim they refer to is found. If lack of unity exists among alternatives within a single claim, separate inventions into groups where practical and relate dependent claims to the alternative they refer to. Note: using the term “invention” is for convenience and does not imply patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of other defects affecting unity
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may refer to other defects (e.g., lack of clarity, prior art leading to a posteriori lack of unity) in addition to or instead of a lack of unity defect, and should explain how those defects impact the assessment of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid confusion about the applicant’s required response, it may be preferable to identify such defects informally (e.g., in the preamble of the report) or explicitly indicate the defect is not being formally identified, solely to explain the impact on assessing unity of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a lack of unity defect should be identified
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of unity of invention should generally be identified in the first report written in respect of the claims that lack unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: if other defects (e.g., obviousness, ambiguity, lack of utility or support) bear on unity and the applicant’s response would be germane, the unity defect may be formally identified in a later report. A lack of unity can be introduced by amendments and may be identified regardless of prior examination length. If prior art suggests a posteriori lack of unity but some claims are anticipated/obvious, it may be preferable to not formally identify lack of unity until the prior art defect is addressed; the applicant may be informed informally. If applicant amends to avoid cited prior art but the amended claims lack unity, the examiner may identify the defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to a requisition identifying lack of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may respond by amending the application to comply with subsection 36(1) of the Patent Act or by submitting arguments that the application already complies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant limits claims to those falling within a single group identified by the examiner, the lack of unity defect will be considered overcome for those claims. The applicant may also identify different groupings and elect among them. If the response does not make the claims compliant with unity requirements, the examiner may send a further report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election of an invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant is considered to have elected an invention when, after a report identifying lack of unity, they limit the claims to fewer inventions than were defined in the claim set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly stating 'I elect Group A' is not necessary. If the initial election limits to a single invention, that defines the 'one invention only' for subsection 36(2). If the initial election selects more than one group (or submits new claims), any further necessary election must be made from among inventions defined in the initially elected claim set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to the Commissioner of Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant declines to limit claims after being notified of a lack of unity defect, the application may be forwarded to the Commissioner for determination, but referral must follow internal review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure efficiency and fairness, an examiner must first submit the application to a Unity Review Board (URB) for review. Possible URB outcomes: (a) unity exists → proceed with substantive exam of all claims; (b) lack of unity exists but further clarification needed → examiner issues further report; (c) lack of unity exists and was clearly communicated → application forwarded to Commissioner. If Commissioner directs limitation (under subsection 36(2.1)), a Notice of Direction is sent. If applicant’s response to the Notice is unsatisfactory, application may be forwarded to the Patent Appeal Board, and refusal will not happen without an opportunity to be heard (per subsection 86(13)). Examiners should expect referral after at least two reports identifying the defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims in different categories presumed to have unity (a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain combinations of claim categories can generally be presumed to satisfy unity of invention when present in a single application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumed category combinations: (a) a product and a process for making that product; (b) a product and a use of that product; (c) a product, a process for making it, and a use; (d) an apparatus and a process carried out on that apparatus. If 'process for making a product' is a 'process carried out on an apparatus,' apparatus claims can be included with product/process/use claims provided the product is inventive by virtue of properties arising from its being prepared using the apparatus. Claim breadth need not be similar to satisfy unity; unity may still exist if scopes differ. Examples illustrate grouping decisions and when claims lack unity a priori or may lack unity a posteriori when prior art is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity when the inventive linking feature is not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of invention may still exist a priori even if the claim language does not explicitly recite the common inventive linking feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a priori assessment examiners should consider the description and common general knowledge before concluding lack of unity. Identify the claim with the fewest elements and check for common elements across independent claims. An applicant may respond to a lack of unity a priori by identifying features they consider the inventive elements common to all claims; the examiner may verify by searching on those elements. Examples show when a linking inventive concept is implicit in the description (and thus unity exists) versus when it is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility of claimed subject-matter (demonstrated or soundly predicted) can inform whether claims form a single invention or multiple inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all embodiments' utility can be soundly predicted using a single line of reasoning based on one set of facts, unity likely exists. If different parts require significantly different sound predictions to support utility, multiple inventions are likely present. A species that has a significantly different utility from the genus may be an aspect of the same invention (if it retains generic utility) or a separate invention (if it replaces the generic utility). Examples clarify when species may be treated as same invention or separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush groups and lists of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush group must define alternatives that are technical equivalents performing the same function in substantially the same way; the skilled person should expect direct substitutability in operable embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for a valid Markush group: (a) each alternative shares a common property or activity and either (i) shares a common structure relevant to activity in the invention, or (ii) belongs to a class recognized in the art where members behave the same way in the invention context. If alternatives do not satisfy these and unity cannot be established by other claim elements, the shared structure or utility must be novel and inventive over prior art to provide unity. Where a list meets the requirements, unity will generally be acknowledged regardless of whether presented as a Markush group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediates and final products
rubrics_metrics.description: An intermediate that is transformed to produce a final product may have unity of invention with the final product despite different inventive steps or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements: the intermediate must necessarily be useful for producing the final product; must share principal structural elements with the final product or introduce an essential structural element; must be a direct precursor to the final product (removed by only one or a few steps) and not a precursor to a known intermediate produced on the way to the final product. Different intermediates that introduce different structural parts will generally not share unity among each other. Chemical examples and detailed analyses illustrate when unity exists (e.g., open-ring precursors sharing core structures) and when certain uses of an intermediate may lack unity with final product claims and thus be appropriate for a divisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-step methods of preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to a single inventive transformative step and claims to larger methods that include that step can share unity; other individual steps that do not include the transformative step may not share unity with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transformative step transforms a precursor into a product and typically shares unity with that product and possibly with certain precursors. Other steps or combinations that do not include the inventive transformative step do not share the general inventive concept and thus do not have unity with it. Products not meeting intermediate/final requirements likewise won't share unity. Example with steps A–E illustrates which combinations have unity based on where the inventive step occurs and how groups can be formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of provisos on unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A proviso (clause excluding matter from a claim) may make claimed subject-matter 'discontinuous' and could remove the general inventive concept, potentially causing lack of unity, but the effect depends on facts and reasons for the proviso.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the reason for the proviso. If used to avoid prior art, determine whether the prior art merely discloses an embodiment within the claim or teaches the same inventive concept. If the latter, unity is likely absent a posteriori; if the former, unity may remain. Example: a genus claim with proviso excluding an earlier species still had unity when the earlier patent had not identified the structure-function relationship that is the inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to file a divisional application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an original application describes more than one invention, the applicant may file a divisional application to protect described inventions other than the one to which the original application’s claims were directed or limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural and administrative requirements and deadlines for filing a divisional are set out elsewhere (see referenced section 3.04). This right derives from subsections 36(2) and 36(2.1) of the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of divisional applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination of divisional applications is similar to regular applications but includes specific checks to ensure the divisional claim set is directed to a different invention and contains no new matter relative to the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the specification and drawings of the divisional to the parent to determine if claims are directed to a different invention and whether the divisional was filed with new matter. If claims are not directed to a different invention than the parent, the later application is not a proper divisional under section 36. If the divisional has a presentation date after October 30, 2019 and contains new matter relative to the parent, it is defective under section 91 or 155.7 of the Patent Rules. Amendments introducing new matter to a divisional invoke subsection 38.2(3.1) of the Patent Act or 155.6 of the Patent Rules (see referenced sections for details). Note: if filing of a divisional was directed by the Patent Office, double-patenting doctrine does not apply between the divisional and its parent/siblings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and purpose of guidance on computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 22 clarifies Office practice for determining whether an invention is statutory and useful when computer-implemented, and elaborates the application of other chapters to issues encountered with computers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'computer' to include processors in various devices (general-purpose CPUs, specific processors, microcontrollers) and may include assemblages of interrelated elements in a single housing. Guidance can apply to servers, PDAs, phones, TVs, appliances, etc. 'Computer' may encompass interacting peripherals (keyboard, display) when referring to general-purpose computers. References to software 'stored on' memory refer to physical memory storing software; no distinction is made between 'stored on' and 'stored in'. Chapter clarifies application of general practice to computer-implemented inventions and does not create exceptions to other chapters.
